title: The highest rung
hookLine: a loan, a partnership or a job, so the person needn't ask again
carry: so they never need to ask

lines: ONCE IT FALLS, IT'S HARD TO LIFT.
cards: A heavy load starts to slip off a donkey's back. One person walking alongside can reach up and steady it. Wait until it crashes to the ground, and even a group will struggle to lift it back.
That picture comes from Rashi, drawing on older teaching, in his commentary on a verse in Leviticus about a brother starting to fall into poverty. Catch it early.
Maimonides builds the top of his ladder on that same verse.

teach.b: The highest rung. In plain English: the greatest level, above which there is none, is to strengthen the hand of someone who has become poor.

teach.h: A GIFT, A LOAN, A PARTNER, A JOB.
teach.b: Give them a gift or a loan, go into partnership with them, or find them work, until they don't need to ask anyone. First, the verse.
Leviticus says, when your brother grows poor and his hand falters beside you, uphold him. In Hebrew, v'hechezakta bo: strengthen him, hold him firm. Maimonides echoes it: strengthen their hand.
Second, the list. A gift, yes. But also a loan, which comes back.
A partnership, where both stand to gain. A job. None of these looks much like charity, and some might even look like business.
He puts them at the top. Third, the aim.

teach.h: END THE NEED, NOT JUST EASE IT.
teach.b: Every lower rung relieves a need. This one ends it. The goal is not that the person feels grateful to you, but that they no longer need you, or anyone.
Fourth, the timing. Remember the donkey. The verse speaks of a hand only beginning to falter.

teach.h: CATCH THE LOAD BEFORE IT FALLS.
teach.b: The highest rung often comes before the fall: the loan that keeps a shop open, the introduction that lands someone work, the partner who shares the risk.

teach.h: SO THEY NEVER NEED TO ASK.
teach.b: It can look ordinary. It might not feel like giving at all. That may be part of why it sits so high.
The person helped keeps their dignity, and walks on.

how: Jewish communities run interest-free loan funds, each called a gemach, and Hebrew Free Loan societies, along with job and business help, as ways of giving at the highest rung.

o: giving the largest sum anyone in town can afford
a gift carved on a plaque at the synagogue door
helping someone stand on their own, so they need no one

games.q: the highest rung — tap the pairs.
p: top-rung giving, though it comes back
the aim of the top rung

s: the highest rung is the biggest donation
it's strengthening someone with a gift, a loan, a partnership or a job.
a job or a partnership can count as top-rung giving
Maimonides lists them alongside a gift and a loan.
the verse behind it speaks of someone whose hand is only beginning to falter
Rashi pictures a load still on the donkey's back: steady it before it falls.

games.q: a friend's small business is slipping. they haven't asked you for anything yet. what would put you on the highest rung?
o: wait until they ask, then give generously.
offer a loan or a partnership that keeps the business standing.
give them some money now, quietly.
games.why: Maimonides' top rung is strengthening the person's hand, by gift, loan, partnership or job, so they won't need to ask anyone.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose hand is faltering a little: a friend looking for work, a neighbor learning something new, a younger colleague.
Ask gently what would strengthen their hand rather than carry them, an introduction, a skill you could teach, a reference, and let one concrete step become clear.

wordCard.voice: The highest rung. In Maimonides' ladder, strengthening someone with a gift, a loan, a partnership or a job, so they won't need to ask anyone. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: and you shall uphold him, from Leviticus 25:35, the verse Maimonides builds the top rung on.

carryVoice: Your line: so they never need to ask. At this height, a good gift works itself out of a job. Back tomorrow, same hill.
